Back when I got it for my PS, my family kept telling me to "just get a PC already" because PS prices were (and maybe still are?) more expensive than PC prices. Honestly, I have no idea how PS game prices stack up against PC games these days, but I have zero regrets; this game was just too much fun.

I vividly recall pausing mid-story for ages just to mess around in free roam. Roaring, turning into dinosaurs, and doing all kinds of random, silly stuff; it was pure joy for me back in the day. Half the time, I didn’t even care about making progress because it was so much fun just playing around. This game was pure bliss and a big part of why gaming felt so magical back then.

Ignore the low hour count for now, because I fully plan to start fresh on my PC once my setup (and life in general) is sorted. Oh, and as a huge fan of the Jurassic World and Jurassic Park movies, this game hits all the right notes. I highly recommend it.

LEGO Jurassic World – How the Roar of Dinosaurs Helped Me Find Myself Again

I had always been a fan of dinosaurs as a kid. From the age of five, I could name almost every species and eagerly awaited the next *Jurassic Park* movie. But somewhere along the way, my love for these prehistoric creatures got buried under the weight of adulthood, responsibility, and the crushing grip of depression. I wasn’t sure where to turn or how to reclaim my joy. Life had become a series of tasks, one after the other, and the world had faded into a gray blur. But then, one day, I decided to give *LEGO Jurassic World* a try, not knowing that it would be the key to pulling me out of my slump and reigniting the spark of wonder I thought I'd lost forever.

At first, I didn’t expect much. I was familiar with LEGO games, and while I had enjoyed them as a child, I figured this would be a light distraction at best. I was deep into my depression, and even the thought of trying something "fun" seemed exhausting. But I needed something to occupy my mind—something that didn’t come with the weight of the world pressing down on me. So, I popped *LEGO Jurassic World* into the console, thinking it might at least be a temporary escape from my daily struggles.

The moment I started the game, I was met with an explosion of color and energy that immediately caught my attention. The opening sequence, set against the iconic *Jurassic Park* theme, was a playful, LEGO-fied tribute to the original film. I instantly recognized the world—the lush jungles of Isla Nublar, the towering, menacing gates of Jurassic Park, the familiar faces of Dr. Alan Grant, Dr. Ellie Sattler, and, of course, John Hammond. The game, with its charming humor and vibrant atmosphere, invited me into a world that was both familiar and fresh. 

But what struck me the most was how the game didn’t just aim to recreate the films; it gave me a new way to experience them. It wasn’t about watching the action unfold—it was about being in the midst of it, running through the park, solving puzzles, unlocking new characters, and, of course, encountering dinosaurs at every turn. The nostalgia hit hard, and for the first time in months, I felt a spark of excitement.

The gameplay itself was straightforward—run, explore, solve puzzles, and collect LEGO studs, but there was something unexpectedly therapeutic about it. It was simple, yes, but in the best way possible. The LEGO world was filled with challenges that required creativity, whether it was using a character’s unique abilities to bypass an obstacle or building structures from LEGO bricks to unlock new paths. Each puzzle I solved gave me a small victory, something I had sorely missed during my depression. Every time I saw my LEGO character crack a joke or make a funny quip, it felt like a little release of tension, a reminder that life didn’t always have to be heavy.

What truly began to heal me, though, were the dinosaurs. They weren’t just creatures roaming the park—they were the heart of the game. The sheer joy of seeing them in all their glory, rendered in LEGO form, was impossible to ignore. From the majestic Brachiosaurus towering over the park to the terrifying, yet oddly lovable, Velociraptors hunting in packs, the dinosaurs became a source of wonder. They were an escape, yes, but they also reminded me of something I had forgotten: the world was full of awe and discovery. And it wasn’t just about the dinosaurs you could see—it was about the dinosaurs you could interact with. 

In the game, I could ride a Triceratops, swim with Plesiosaurs, and even take control of the mighty T. rex. Each moment spent with these creatures was a brief but powerful reminder that there was more to life than the grayness I had been trapped in. The joy of exploring Isla Nublar, unlocking new areas, and encountering new species was contagious. I was a part of something bigger, something grand and exciting. The world of *LEGO Jurassic World* was alive, and for the first time in a long time, I felt alive too.

The game’s open-world structure also allowed me to take my time. I could wander the park, revisit areas I had already explored, and uncover hidden secrets. There was no rush. No deadlines. No pressure. It was just me, my dinosaurs, and the freedom to roam at my own pace. This lack of pressure was the most freeing thing about the game. In the real world, everything felt like it was moving too fast. Every day, I felt like I was running behind, overwhelmed by expectations and responsibilities. But here, in *LEGO Jurassic World*, I could slow down. I could take a breath. I could enjoy the journey.

I found comfort in the simple act of exploring, of allowing myself to be curious again. As I unlocked new characters, including some of the most iconic figures from the films, I felt like I was unlocking pieces of myself that I had buried away. I began to remember what it was like to be excited about something—anything—beyond the daily grind. The joy of discovery, the thrill of encountering something new, even the smallest LEGO building puzzle—it all started to bring a sense of fulfillment and hope back into my life. Each new challenge became a stepping stone toward healing, a reminder that there was always something worth striving for, something worth enjoying, even in the midst of a storm.

One of the most powerful moments came when I finally unlocked the T. rex. It’s one of the most iconic dinosaurs in *Jurassic Park*, and in the game, it was a force to be reckoned with. The roar of the T. rex, the way it charged through the park, smashing obstacles in its path—it was both thrilling and cathartic. For a brief moment, I felt like I was that T. rex. I wasn’t helpless or small anymore. I could crush the obstacles in my path, face the challenges head-on, and feel unstoppable. It wasn’t just about the game. It was about the feeling it gave me—empowerment, freedom, and a sense of strength I had forgotten I possessed.

As I continued to play, I realized that the game wasn’t just providing me with a temporary escape. It was helping me build my resilience. The puzzles were often tricky, but I didn’t give up. The dinosaurs were fierce, but I learned how to navigate around them. The game was teaching me that life—like a Jurassic park—was full of unexpected twists and turns. But that didn’t mean I couldn’t face them. I didn’t have to be perfect. I just had to keep going, one step at a time.

By the time I reached the end of the main story, I was a different person. The weight of depression still lingered, but it no longer had a hold on me. I had rediscovered my curiosity, my sense of play, and my capacity for joy. *LEGO Jurassic World* had given me something more than just a fun game—it had shown me that there was still beauty, excitement, and wonder in the world. It had reminded me that it was okay to take things slow, to enjoy the ride, and to be kind to myself along the way.

The game’s colorful landscapes, the thrill of dinosaur encounters, and the satisfaction of solving puzzles had helped me rediscover something crucial: *I was still capable of feeling joy*. Looking at Steamdb, the game goes on sale quite a bit, usually for like 80% off, so maybe wait for a sale to buy it.

- The LEGO environments mixed with more realistic and non-LEGO stuff is jarring and pretty ugly. I think everything should be LEGO in a LEGO game.
- The game is obviously a tie-in for the first JW movie and the devs have put most of their effort into the JW levels, which in turn makes the remaining JP levels feel a little bit empty and small.

It's still alright though. Get it for 10 dollars or less and you're set.

Here is a link for you to check. A bug for over 8 years now.

https://www.playstationtrophies.org/forum/topic/251038-lego-jurassic-world-all-known-glitches-with-solutions/

[h1][b] Pros? [/b][/h1]
⚫LEGO® Jurassic World is fully finished. You get to play 4 full lego games in the one more or less and you get to experience all of what Jurassic Park has to offer.
⚫There is no OVERPRICED character skin packs costing £29.99 for 10 characters.
⚫Got the GOOD music soundtrack to it and not some random garbage to replace the actual theme song.
⚫Fun for the entire family at any age!

[h1][b] My Verdict [/b][/h1]
All in all, I can recommend LEGO® Jurassic World because you can see that they have tried to flesh out many issues from previous lego games but in return they have caused some new ones trying to perfect it. LEGO Jurassic World – A Dino-Sized Adventure in Brick Form
After spending 27.6 hours in LEGO Jurassic World, I can confidently say it’s a fun, nostalgia-filled journey that captures the magic of the films while keeping true to the signature LEGO humor and charm.

Gameplay & Exploration
The game takes you through all four Jurassic films, letting you relive iconic moments with a comedic LEGO twist. The open-world hub areas—Isla Nublar and Isla Sorna—offer plenty of exploration, side quests, and hidden collectibles. While the gameplay follows the classic LEGO formula (smash everything, collect studs, solve simple puzzles), the addition of dinosaurs makes it stand out. Being able to control and even customize dinosaurs adds an extra layer of fun.

Graphics & Sound
The environments are surprisingly well-detailed, capturing the jungle-like atmosphere of Jurassic Park. The use of original voice clips from the movies is a nice touch, but at times, the audio feels a bit off due to its direct lift from the films. Still, the iconic John Williams score playing in the background never gets old.

Story & Humor
As expected from a LEGO game, the story follows the movies but with a lighthearted, comedic spin. Whether it’s the goofy expressions, slapstick gags, or ridiculous reinterpretations of serious scenes, it keeps things entertaining. Fans of the franchise will enjoy the nods to the films, while younger players will appreciate the humor and simple storytelling.

Replayability & Content
100% completion will take some dedication, with tons of collectibles, hidden dinosaurs, and extra challenges. While the levels are linear, free play mode allows you to go back with different characters and abilities to unlock secrets. However, if you’re used to LEGO games, you might find the gameplay a bit repetitive after a while.

Final Verdict
⭐ 8/10 – LEGO Jurassic World is a solid LEGO game, perfect for fans of both the franchise and the LEGO series. While the gameplay can get repetitive, the mix of dinosaur action, humor, and nostalgia makes it a worthwhile adventure. Completing it in 27.6 hours felt like a well-spent journey through Jurassic history, brick by brick.

For as long as we have existed, there has been one fact of life that has stood the test of time: kids love dinosaurs. Always have, always will. So for TT to make a game based on the Jurassic Park IP, a series all about said dinosaurs, is a no brainer. I've only ever seen the first film and played 1998's infamous FPS game Trespasser, so I have very little connection to the series beyond that, but that didn't stop me from having fun with this game. 

It's your fairly typical LEGO affair, covering the first four films in the series. There's a large collection of characters that are unlocked by completing each film's levels, although if you asked me who most of them were I'd be clueless. Each minikit represents the bones of a dinosaur, which become playable once you unlock them. The stud multipliers are very easy to get, with me being able to achieve x3840 pretty quickly, which makes purchasing everything a breeze.

When you unlock different dinosaurs in each level, you can customise them to your liking, making entirely new species to roam around the park with their own abilities which are convenient for Free Play. I even made one based on my cat. The standard 1M stud level is present as always, although this game's catch is that you won't actually be able to play it until you reach 100% completion. Instead of that as the bonus, you will find bonus levels across the different parks, although most of these are just taken straight from the actual levels.

There may be some expense spared in some areas, but I'm sure this is one park LEGO and Jurassic fans alike would be happy to endorse.

LEGO Jurassic World is exactly what you'd hope for: dinosaurs, chaos, and that signature LEGO charm all rolled into one dino-sized adventure. Whether you’re a lifelong Jurassic Park fan or just love running around as a tiny blocky T. rex, this game delivers.

The best part? It covers all four films from the original Jurassic Park trilogy and Jurassic World. That means you get to relive the most iconic scenes—from the T. Rex breakout and raptor kitchen scene to Owen Grady wrangling raptors like a boss. And all of it is done with LEGO's trademark humour, clever slapstick, and surprisingly great attention to detail.

The environments are beautifully crafted in that colourful, LEGO-fied way. From Isla Nublar’s lush jungle to the high-tech facilities of Jurassic World, each area feels alive and full of secrets to uncover. And yes—you can play as dinosaurs. That’s not a drill. You can stomp around as a triceratops, roar as a T. Rex, and even build your own custom dinos. It’s silly, it’s fun, and it never gets old.

There’s a huge roster of characters from across all the movies, each with different abilities, and tons of collectables, gold bricks, puzzles, and side activities to keep you busy. The game also has great couch co-op, making it perfect for playing with friends or family. It’s accessible enough for kids but nostalgic and fun enough for older fans.

I think Lego games that feature ‘ordinary’ human people are significantly less fun than ones that feature super-powered people. What could be so interesting about playing as a bunch of people whose abilities are “hitting things with their hands” and who are differentiated by the type of machines they can operate? Corporate workers can access certain computers, intellectuals can solves puzzle boards, archaeologists can put bones together or dive into piles of poo… but you wouldn’t know from looking at them because they all look like ordinary Lego people. In fact, this is the first game in the franchise I’ve noticed where the characters’ abilities are written underneath their names!

Still, the developer treats all these franchises with respect and good-natured humour, and I do enjoy the family-friendly visual comedy they add to the scenes. Even that poor tortured woman from Jurassic World survives inside the mouth of the mosasaurus!

Traveler's Tales' LEGO series, based on various licensed properties, has become somewhat of a staple in many video game collections since its inception with the the 'LEGO Star Wars' games, so after seeing 'Jurassic World' I was ready to go through the LEGO tie-in game, and after a couple of days, I've been left with a dissappointing experience.

There have been many other reviews already talking about the plethora of bugs within the game, and I ran into quite a few myself, two of which halted my progress and forced me to restart the levels I found them on, one of them prevented me from building something because I previously broke some nearby boxes, which is very counterintuitive for a bloody lego game.

However, they also included voice acting for this one, and whilst it's heartwarming to hear Jeff goldblums' laugh (and voice in general) come out of a LEGO figure, the age of the audio become apparent, since it's taken from the original 'Jurassic Park' so the difference in quality between audio from 2015 and 1993 is seen rather easily.

This leads to another problem with the game. It isn't funny. Aside from a chuckle or two I got from the raptors and their shenanigans, none of the humour appealed to me. This is partially to blame on the inclusion of voice acting, since the strength of previous LEGO titles was the physical comedy, it was probably one of the main reasons I loved the LEGO series, but it's been diminished significantly in favour of mediocre verbal comedy, which takes away quite a bit of enjoyment from the game.

The game is strangely anti-death aswell, but I won't dwell too much on that, just know that nodoby dies in LEGO jurassic world, including one character who survived being eaten by being thrown back up a short while later.

However, there is fun to be had in LEGO Jurassic World, the gameplay is as strong as ever, it's still the standard LEGO game affair, smash everything and anything breakable in sight, and attentively searching the levels for the minikits (Most of which are well placed) still manages to be both fun and challenging. A lot of detail has also been put into the open world aspect of it. There's also the option to play as dinosaurs, which is as epic as it sounds!

On the whole though, it's a bit of a mediocre experience for me, but would I recommend the game? Short answer: Probably not. If you love the other LEGO games, you'll probably like this one (If it works for you), however, if your new to the LEGO games, don't buy this one. Get 'LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga' Instead, It's not as buggy, cheaper, funnier and is based on a better film franchise.

TL;DR: Dissappointing. Weak humour, but still has good lego collectathon style gameplay. Not even Jeff Goldblum and playing as a T-Rex could save this one.

Final Score: 6/10

Lego Jurassic World is yet another yet another yet another LEGO game from Traveller's Tales factory of Lego. Yep, 3D casual platformer based on license. Released in 2015, based on all 4 Jurassic Park movies. It also was released for PS3, PS4, Xbox 360, Xbox One and WiiU. Yes, PC wasn't cut in any way, so everything is good. It also had handheld release for 3DS and Vita, which is your usual lesser, yet different enough that fans might check those out. Maybe.

But first thing you must do before playing this game is to go to options and switch DirectX from 11 to 9. There are too many reports of glitches exclusive to DirectX 11. Even more, it seems that game's saves are tied to DirectX. As in, I seen reports that people were not able to load their old save which they switched from 11 to 9. So yea, do that immeditly.
Those who still have various progress-halting bugs are also recommended to activate V-Sync. It actually fixed some things in old Lego games too.

And yea, like other recent Lego games, it's still is full of various bugs, from crashes to getting stuck in geometry. Personally, it glitched on me on the first launch, where it got stuck in background process and I couldn't end it, so I had to reboot PC. And the final scenes in final level seemed showed me some wonky collision glitches that I was worried that the game is about to just break down like a card construction. Made of lego.

I also recommend using gamepad. Was designed for that. At least it would make circular cranes less annoying, as on gamepad you are supposed to circle analog around.

Anyway, it's yet another Lego game. You know what I mean. Casual. Can't die. Punch things. Hold button to build out of some things you punched. Collect studs. Feel yourself having OCD.
It's good. It's stale.

Nothing much new there. Dinos. Bringing minigames and such from previous Lego titles. I don't think that this one has any new one. Well, maybe "repeat input" one for various terminals or such.

It also keeps the usual Lego charm. In this one no one technically dies. No one important and in cutscene, that is. Which is fancy. Waiting for Rampage Edition though.

Gameplay is also isn't focused on combat which is pretty much always a good thing in Lego games from Travellers Tales. Albeit when it does, it's probably a flock of those annoying tiny dinos that swarm you and each takes two hits to takedown. Which isn't exactly fun. But at least the game is fast paced. In a sense that it keeps moving on at about time it's about to get really boring.

Anyway, it's kinda good. Brings nothing new. I liked music at least. But I am never buying a new Lego game ever again. Because it's stale in no end.

If you like the lego games, you'll likely enjoy Lego Jurassic World.  It doesn't change the formula in the slightest.  This has its upsides and its downsides because of it.  

Pros:
Classic Lego gameplay.  You break stuff, you collect studs, you build things, you solve rudementary puzzles, it's all the classic lego games, just with a jurassic park skin.

Stories are handled rather well.  They (mostly) keep true to the stories, they're presented in a fun way, it's well done.

Classic Lego humor is back.  Lego Marvel was lacking a lot of the classic lego slapstick, this has brought it back.  Characters do silly things, there are plenty of visual gags to laugh at.

You get to play as dinosaurs (some of them, see cons for an explaination)  


Cons:
Let's get the big one out of the way, it's glitchy.  This is the glitchiest Lego game I've ever played.  There are puzzles that require raptors to jump on certain things.  I believe there are 5 times you have to do this in the story.  Of the 5 times I tried it, 4 had the raptors getting stuck in midair.  Waiting about 30 seconds finished the animation and I thankfully didn't have to restart any of the levels, but I was dreading each time I'd have to do the raptor jump to progress the game.  I've also had issues with characters getting stuck on objects, compies not being able to get out of tubes, animations glitching out.  It's a glitchy game.  I personally didn't have any gamebreaking glitches, but the ones I experienced certainly had the potential to be gamebreaking.

The voice acting.  This is a problem I've had with every lego game since they started with it in Lego Lord of the Rings.  I don't like the voice acting in lego games to begin with, it works much better in games like Lego Star Wars where the stories are told purely visually.  Lego Jurassic World is the worst of the worst when it comes to voice acting.  Like in the lord of the rings, they decided to use clips of audio taken directly from the movies.  I'm not sure if they were aware of this while making hte game, but sound quality in movies from the 1990s wasn't exactly very good.  It's even more apparent when there are background npcs that have freshly recorded lines form the 2010s.  The difference is instantly noticable, and it's really really badly done.  

Strangly anti-death.  In a video game series full of comedic violence and cartoonish death scenes, it's strange to see the lego games go so anti-death with Jurassic Park.  No one dies in the game.  All the people that get eaten don't actually die.  They either get tickled by raptors, or if they do get eaten by a T-Rex, they are vomited out by the end, totally unharmed. Anyway, here's my review, still intact and unchanged.

Until this game receives a patch, I cannot recommend purchasing this. I'll go over what I liked first:

- The gameplay is exactly what you'd expect from Lego games. Run around, break things, collect studs, solve puzzles, collect bricks, grind your way towards 100% completion. If you've been liking past Lego games, you'll feel right at home with the gameplay here.

- Like all Lego games of this type, it's a very faithful and humorous re-telling of the four movies it covers. There are a lot of humorous moments, and a lot of the cracks it makes at the movies had me laughing a fair bit.

- The graphics are gorgeous. It's colorful and detailed, as you'd expect from Lego games.

- The free roam areas are pretty awesome. Though they are a bit linear, they are full of things to do, and the amount of detail put into them is incredible. There's a free roam map for each movie, allowing for a good amount of variety.

All-in-all, the game itself is great. However, it's held back by an awful amount of bugs. Here's just a few of what I've encountered:

- In one level, a couple of the NPCs simply floated off into the sky for no particular reason.

- A few chase levels have the dinosaur chasing you glitch out, so it disappears, and you're left with nothing chasing you.

- One red brick wouldn't appear until I restarted my game.

- One red brick DID appear before I even attempted to do a puzzle because my AI partner somehow squeezed himself into the final part of the puzzle.

- In a couple of levels, I randomly fell through the floor, falling forever.

- Several times, I got stuck in some of the background, making progress impossible without restarting the level.

- There have been some invisible walls in various areas, particuarly in the green tubes that the small dinos use. Some have literally been impossible to exit because of random invisible walls.

- Some of the raptor jump levers literally will not let you all the way up onto the platforms you're trying to reach, so you have to fight the controls and the background a bit to finally push yourself up.

- In one bonus level where you play as the Indominous Rex, it literally does not appear, so you can't do anything.

- I rescued a Worker In Peril, but it didn't count towards the peril count for some reason, and now the game is acting like she's there when she's not, rendering 100% completion impossible.

- The game has crashed on me several times.

That's just what comes off the top of my head. There may be more I'm forgetting. One or two glitches, I can understand, but this game is literally plain unfinished. The developers rushed this through the gates without even so much as doing a simple bug-test. A lot of these bugs are things you'll find just through doing a normal playthrough of the game.

I've nearly completed the game, but I can't get 100% because of the missing worker. This playthrough has had its moments of fun, but it's also been nothing short of irritating and mind-boggingly tedious.

If and when a patch comes out, I'd say get this game, but until then, save your money.

Very disappointing. This game has to be the most "child friendly" Lego game I've played, not only refusing to show the deaths that occured in the movies, but going so far as to dedicate scenes to how all these canonically dead characters survived. Fat dude who got gooed in the face? Nah, he's fine. Black dude who was just an arm? All there, just frozen like a statue for some unexplained reason. Guy killed on the toilet? Nah, coughed up later. It goes beyond comedy, actively removing any sense of danger or respect to the source. For Lego, a style that can actively show characters losing limbs or being popped in half without any sense of gore or violence, this seems like needless pandering. Why would a child play this game if they haven't seen the movies? If they've seen the movies, they'll have seen the deaths. If they haven't seen the movies, they'll want to after playing this, so what is acheived? Explain to me how horrific seeing a disembodied Lego arm would really be - you could even have it worm its way off screen after to retain the lightheartedness, but cencoring all harm is just insulting.

Each movie is about 5 missions, which makes each one feel EXTREMELY short and truncated. You'll get to play all your favourite scenes, but expect to play ONLY those, and expect them to be warped to suit the gameplay. There's also a bizzare mix of audio (extremely obviously) cut from the movies for the big names, while lesser characters are voiced by studio-quality imitators. In my opinion, it should be all or nothing, not snippets here and there like some fan-made Flash game.

The gold bricks are EXTREMELY easy to aquire, usually no more complex than "do you have the right character? then press a button to receive". There are no quests like the Marvel games, no interesting dialogue or mini stories, you just go to the gold brick on the map and do the one thing. And don't let the long list of activities fool you, each race or dinosaur healing only gives you a gold brick, so each one ticks off two things at once. It is a prime example of the illusion of content, while it is infact just repetative tasks and progression-blocked interactions. If you speed through the story missions and finish the game, giving you access to all the skills, I beleive you could get all the world-map bricks in a handful of hours.

Now this game is nowhere near as short as the Lego Movie game, but it's shaping up to the be second shortest. Like the Lego Movie game however, this one feels like a cheap and soulless cash-in. The new voiceovers sound bored and lifeless, the levels are repetative break-and-build situations, while the actual content barely resembles the movies and half of the character list are generic nobodies you've never heard of and reskins for Park/World. On top of that, the lego versions of these characters are wholly unrecognisable besides a couple of main characters, and more than once I had to google the character's name to figure out who they were supposed to be. I fully understand the reductionist Lego style, but once again I've never had this problem with other lego games, further evidence to me that this is just another lazy movie cash-in.

Being able to play as (and edit) dinosaurs makes up for a lot, and on that merit alone it may be worth getting for a lot of people, but this is by no means a great game, and it feels like a big step backwards for the Lego series. If you're simply looking for a good Lego game, pick a different one. If you're a big Jurassic fan, prepare to be underwhelmed, but you'll probably find enough to enjoy the game.

Don't get me wrong, this is a "good" LEGO game and has it's moments and it's mostly there, however I would suggest getting this with a hefty discount (90%) if you can as full price is not warranted for this "almost complete" game.

So the good first:
It's a standard LEGO game with all that has been come to expect of a LEGO game.
Decent array of characters and the fact you can play as dinosaurs too is a fun quirk.

Story is all there - playing the game I remembered the movies scene for scene, so it definitely hit all the right marks.

Decent length, around 20 hours to 100%.

-------
Now for the bad and the reason I don't suggest it without a discount:

Main menu - is obviously not complete! doesn't look nice and has some weird quirks with some random menus coming from random directions and some just glide over the entire screen.

Controls screen - just don't! seriously don't look at that screen, it's so badly laid out.

Audio options - just volume, no individual control [i]You'll see why that's important in a second[/i]

Gameplay - mostly okay.
However some controls are janky AF - the velociraptor ledge jumping is a prime example, 9 times out of 10 it would fail to work. In the case of one of the story levels it just refused to work and I spent a good 20 minuets just trying to jump up one ledge that would catch but then you'd just fall down, it was a very fussy ledge!

Camera controls - sometimes bugs out, but it was rare.


[i]But wait, there's more....[/i]
Now for the most annoying issues!

Overlay bug / game progress lost - This took me by surprise once I realised what was going on. If you are completing something like a gold brick collection / worker saved etc... and you traverse area's in free-roam [i](not a level)[/i] before it finishes rendering the game get's stuck in a situation that doesn't resolve until you start a level.
The overlay will no longer trigger for subsequent actions, like picking up a gold brick but it says nothing, but the pause menu shows progress. If you then fast travel to somewhere else in free-roam and then come back, that thing you just collected would still be there and your progress will have been reset.

The fix is to start a level and either complete it or just back out back to the island and all should be well again.
I thought this was a weird one but encountered it 3 times naturally and 3 more times while I was testing what was causing the problem to confirm my issue! - you have been warned.


Now for my biggest complaint - the campaign audio!
The audio clips in this game sound like they were taken from a badly pirated copy of the original movies [i](they are original movie audio though)[/i], and just jammed into this game. It's clear that no time was spent on cleaning these up before release as the audio is all over the place and really detracts from the game-play.
The clips aren't audio balanced, so some clips are very quiet and others (sometimes instantly preceding a quiet clip) are really loud, like they've been turned up to 11!

The instance that caused me to just turn my volume right down, [i](as there's no individual audio options)[/i], was when during a cut-scene the audio was quiet, then super loud, then the background music randomly became super loud and I couldn't hear the characters talk at all - it was enough to force me to panic turn down my speakers and so off putting for game-play!

It's clear this game didn't have a final polish applied before it was released which to me was such a let down.

-------
Overall it's a good LEGO game, but as I suggested at the start, only bug this if it has a serious discount!

TLDR; Despite there being a couple very unique and good things about the game, i still can't recommend LEGO Jurassic World because the negatives overpower the positives. It wasn't that memorable or enjoyable of an experience in the late portions of the game. The story was pleasant to go through, playing as dinos felt unique for a LEGO game, although it had overused sequences such as the chase/flee ones. And the outdated options/settings made the game be an annoyance in certain levels. It definitely required a bit more polish before it's release date back in 2015.



[h1] The Good: [/h1]
- The game features the movies Jurassic Park 1-3 and Jurassic World itself, in a LEGOified humorous setting with each movie having 5-6 story levels. All story characters are also voice acted with most lines being pulled from the movies, with some also made only for the game.

- After completing a movie's story levels, it's "hub" area becomes fully accessible and discoverable. These contain collectibles such as Gold Bricks, Red Bricks (buyable cheats basically), saving people, curing dinos, taking photographs of set locations, and even racing with vehicles and dinosaurs.

- In traditional fashion, completed story levels can also be accessed via free play, where you can play as any character you'd like to collect all 10 minikits in a level alongside the Amber DNA of dinos.

- A unique aspect of this game is that you can play as dinosaurs. Most of them have their own unique abilities which will aid you in the story, the freely roamable hubs and replayable levels of the game.

- As with any other LEGO game, you can mix&match other unlocked LEGO character's parts to create your own LEGO character.

- Alongside this, you can also create your own dinosaur with parts of other unlocked dinos you collect through Ambers.

- The progression felt great. The amount of money (studs) gained from props is less in this game than what you'd expect from other various LEGO games. Getting currency felt way better and more valuable until you get Red Bricks that accelerate your progress. (i.e. 2-4-6-8-10x money multipliers) To get actually meaningful Red Bricks you had to play through a large chunk of the story first to unlock character abilities which you'd be able to unlock said Red Bricks with.



[h1] The Bad: [/h1]
- Playing on too high of an FPS/Hz breaks the game. The game breaks in many parts if you play above 60Hz / 60FPS. In my case i was playing on 240Hz with Vsync on (and i recommend Vsync on) and the physics broke often. Examples are; in a few levels it can break the AI, some missions the scripted event's movement was way slower than with less fps, dino charging into orange Amber bricks and green Toxic props sent my dino flying up in the sky.

- Tabbing out always resets your game's refresh rate to your monitor's lowest supported refresh rate. The game also has no Windowed Fullscreen mode.

- Most dialogues were taken from the movies themselves, with them feeling out of place, not polished and often times very quiet. Audio balancing needed some more work. The audio settings also only have one global sound slider and a music toggle on/off, nothing else in terms of audio. Which is a shame because the music was way louder over everything else many times.

- Played it on a keyboard yet i still got controller hints on certain actions. (i.e. driving hints)

- The places/ways of getting Minikits felt unoriginal/uncreative. Few of them were given to you just by progressing the game, many were just shooting X things Y times, and another couple were through chase sequences. There weren't many special areas in free play.

- Talking about chase/flee sequences, they were the worst, most annoying and overused part of the game. There were about 12 of them total in the whole game. If you were going for 100% completion, then collecting minikits in these were painful. The camera angle... wasn't in the favour of the players sort to say, so it lead to trial and errors to get the Minikits in these portions of the levels.

- I know it's because of the movies, but characters just all felt the same, and did not feel special.

- The game's length could've been longer.
Don't Buy this until a couple weeks from now, because there are a lot of game breaking bugs that might get patched, but that depends on the developers
